gates.label: Price above 50-day average
gates.explain: The price is higher than its average over the last 50 trading days. A stock below its recent average is drifting down, and the system will not buy a falling stock.

gates.label: Price above 200-day average
gates.explain: The price is higher than its average over the last 200 trading days, about ten months. This is the long-term direction check.

gates.label: 20-day average above 50-day average
gates.explain: The short-term average sits above the medium-term one, which means the recent move is up, not just the long-run one.

gates.label: 20-day momentum positive
gates.explain: The price is higher than it was 20 trading days ago, roughly one month.

gates.label: Not stretched: under 15% above the 50-day average
gates.explain: A stock that has run far above its own average often snaps back. The system refuses to chase it.

gates.label: Forecast model gives over 62% odds of a higher price
gates.explain: A statistical forecasting model estimates the chance the price is higher in about a month. Below 62% the system treats the signal as too weak.

gates.label: No volatility spike
gates.explain: Day-to-day price swings over the last month are not far above their recent norm. A sudden jump in swings usually means news the system has not priced.

gates.label: Not already held
gates.explain: The practice account does not already own it, so a buy would be a new position rather than doubling up.

gates.label: Enough cash left after the buy
gates.explain: After a standard-size buy the account would still hold more than 10% cash, so one position cannot drain it.

gates.label: Its sector stays under 40% of the book
gates.explain: Adding it would not push one industry past 40% of the portfolio. Too much in one sector means one bad headline hits everything at once.

gates.label: Altman Z-score of 1.81 or higher
gates.explain: The Altman Z-score is a standard 1968 formula that uses five ratios from the balance sheet and income statement to flag companies at risk of financial distress. Below 1.81 is the distress zone.

gates.label: Beneish M-score of -1.78 or lower
gates.explain: The Beneish M-score is a 1999 formula that looks for patterns in the accounts that often appear when earnings are being manipulated. Above -1.78 is a warning sign.

gates.label: Price no more than 25% above estimated fair value
gates.explain: The system estimates what the company is worth from its cash flows. It will not buy a company priced far above that estimate, however good the trend looks.

companies.name: Eaton
companies.thesis: Makes the electrical gear (switchgear, transformers, power distribution) the AI buildout runs on. Data-center and grid electrification demand is filling a multi-year backlog, which is the Silicon-Power Gap thesis turning into orders.

companies.name: Quanta Services
companies.thesis: Builds and upgrades the electric grid itself. The transmission bottleneck the SPG paper identifies is exactly what Quanta gets paid to relieve, so constrained supply is a tailwind, not a risk.

companies.name: Comfort Systems
companies.thesis: Mechanical and electrical contractor building the guts of data centers. Rising data-center construction flows straight into its backlog and margins.

companies.name: GE Vernova
companies.thesis: Sells the transformers, turbines, and grid hardware the SPG thesis argues are supply-constrained. A pure expression of the high-voltage equipment shortage.

companies.name: Vistra
companies.thesis: Independent power producer with nuclear and gas capacity. Sells the electricity AI data centers are bidding up, and benefits directly from rising power prices.

companies.name: Constellation Energy
companies.thesis: Largest US nuclear fleet. Clean 24/7 baseload is the scarce input for always-on AI compute, and Constellation is already signing data-center power deals.

companies.name: NRG Energy
companies.thesis: Retail and generation power gaining pricing power as US electricity demand growth returns after two flat decades, led by data centers.

companies.name: NVIDIA
companies.thesis: The demand engine of the whole thesis. Its accelerators create the electricity and grid strain that makes every power and equipment name in this list matter.

companies.name: Broadcom
companies.thesis: AI networking and custom accelerators. The second pick-and-shovel of the compute buildout alongside NVDA, with stickier enterprise revenue.

companies.name: TSMC
companies.thesis: Manufactures essentially all leading-edge AI chips. The foundry chokepoint upstream of all AI compute demand, with near-monopoly economics.

companies.name: Iron Mountain
companies.thesis: Storage business funding a fast-growing data-center arm. Owns the physical real estate AI compute has to live in.

companies.name: Digital Realty
companies.thesis: Pure-play data-center REIT and landlord to the hyperscalers driving power demand. Rents rise as capacity gets scarce.

companies.name: Equinix
companies.thesis: Interconnection-led data-center REIT where cloud, AI, and networks meet. High switching costs and pricing power as AI traffic grows.

companies.name: Vertiv
companies.thesis: Thermal management and power distribution for data centers. Cooling is the second bottleneck behind transformers as rack density explodes.

companies.name: Super Micro
companies.thesis: Builds the AI server racks NVIDIA chips ship in. A direct read on data-center buildout velocity, with thinner margins and higher cyclicality.

companies.name: Dell Technologies
companies.thesis: Enterprise AI server and storage demand. A steadier, lower-multiple way to play the same compute buildout as SMCI.

companies.name: Arista Networks
companies.thesis: High-speed switching that wires AI clusters together. Networking is the unglamorous chokepoint inside the data center; Arista owns the high end.

companies.name: Hubbell
companies.thesis: Electrical and utility infrastructure components. A diversified pick-and-shovel on grid electrification alongside ETN and GEV.

companies.name: Powell Industries
companies.thesis: Switchgear and electrical distribution for utilities, energy, and data centers. A small-cap, high-torque expression of the power-equipment shortage.

companies.name: Atkore
companies.thesis: Electrical conduit and cable management — the plumbing every data center and grid project consumes. Cyclical but cash-generative.

companies.name: Entergy
companies.thesis: Regulated utility serving Gulf-South industrial and data-center load growth, nuclear in the mix. Rate-base growth as demand returns.

companies.name: Southern Company
companies.thesis: Large Southeast utility with new Vogtle nuclear capacity online — clean baseload exactly where data-center load is migrating.

companies.name: American Electric Power
companies.thesis: Owns the largest US transmission network. The grid bottleneck the SPG thesis identifies is AEP's multi-decade rate-base opportunity.

companies.name: Talen Energy
companies.thesis: Independent power producer with nuclear already contracted to hyperscalers for data-center power. A pure behind-the-meter AI-power play.

companies.name: NuScale Power
companies.thesis: SMR developer — the speculative long-dated option on next-gen clean baseload for AI. High risk, asymmetric if small modular reactors scale.
